books.title: The Denial of Death
books.author: Ernest Becker
books.fullReview:
To begin this journey into the depths of depth psychology and existentialism, we start with The Denial of Death by Ernest Becker. This book took me about a week, and I had some experiences along the way because of the revelations Becker so generously shares — the culmination of a life’s work in 284 pages. Consider me a rookie in the field of social science and psychology. I am one. But I can’t hold back: I think this is an astonishing, world-altering masterpiece.

I’d known about the book for years, and I think I even started it once and bailed. This year I finally picked up the 50th anniversary edition — mine has a new foreword by physicist Brian Greene, who’s written elsewhere about Becker’s influence on him.I read almost all of it in a few days. When I reached the final chapter, I stopped. I was still processing Parts I and II. The detail Becker goes into on Freud, Jung, Kierkegaard, and Rank is captivating — I learned so much about all four of these thinkers and their contributions. In these exciting bursts, Becker is never afraid to rebuke a giant or make a grand statement. Reading them, I kept feeling a low-grade unease. Am I going to learn something in this book I don’t want to know? Some terrifying truth? I felt a gradual shift in how I think about life and myself that I’m still adjusting to — this dualism of the animal body and the symbolic self, at odds with one another. I’d felt that split before. I just never had language for it.


Where the name comes from
You may have noticed that the Substack you are reading is called An Anus that Shits. This I lifted from a passage early in the book. Sorry ladies. 

“to fashion the sublime miracle of the human face, the mysterium tremendum of radiant feminine beauty, the veritable goddesses that beautiful women are; to bring out of nothing, out of the void, and make it shine in noonday; to take such a miracle and put miracles again within it, deep in the mysetery of eyes that peer out —the eye that gave even the dry Darwin a chill: to do all this, and to combine it with an anus that shits!”

So let me explain my own anality, since the name demands it.
I remember, at three or four years old, smearing shit on a toilet and sink at my aunt and uncle’s house. I remember smearing it on Barbie dolls, of all items, too — a memory I didn’t actually have until years later, going through old boxes of toys, when I found a Barbie with shit crusted on her and thought, with total confidence, I believe that this shit is mine! Incredible that I unlocked such a distant memory. Fascinating and amazing, really.

I know this is unpleasant for anyone who has fully repressed, forgotten, or denies their own anality to this day. Freud was cult-like in demanding his theory be the final word on human psychology, and he was quick to make grand, sometimes overly simplistic claims about behavior rooted in sexuality. Fair criticism. But having actually gone and read up on the “anal stage,” I can say it’s a more serious observation about human nature than the cartoon version of Freud gets credit for.

Freud placed the anal stage roughly between eighteen months and three years old — the window when toilet training turns the bowels into the first real site of a child’s control over their own body. His 1908 essay “Character and Anal Erotism” argued that this early fixation on holding and releasing doesn’t just vanish; it gets sublimated into adult character traits — orderliness, stinginess, obstinacy, an interest in money and possession that Freud read as displaced interest in what the body once withheld or expelled. Later analysts like Karl Abraham split this further into an expulsive phase (hostile, destructive) and a retentive phase (controlling, hoarding), and the theory has had a long life in the literature since, right up through people using it to explain everything from misers to obsessives like Jonathan Swift, who Becker discusses at length as a man horrified by his own body’s animality.

But Becker doesn’t leave it there, and this is the part that actually rearranged something in my head. Leaning on the psychoanalyst Norman O. Brown, Becker strips anality out of the strictly sexual frame Freud built it in and reads it as existential instead. It isn’t really about the anus. It’s about what the anus proves: that you are an animal that will die, wrapped in an identity that believes it’s more than an animal. The disgust we feel toward excretion isn’t juvenile squeamishness — it’s the body reminding the symbolic self, the part of you that writes essays and falls in love and plans a future, that it’s still an animal sitting on its own filth. “On the highest throne in the world,” Montaigne wrote, “man sits on his arse.” Becker’s argument is that culture itself — art, ambition, religion, money, all of it — is in part a fabricated protest against that fact. A way of forgetting what we are. That reframe is why the name of this newsletter isn’t a joke, or not only a joke. It’s the whole thesis on a marquee.

The river

I’ve been going down to the park by the river to read. I was there finishing the eleventh chapter and got overcome — the water, the sky, even the power plant and the bridge to the east looked beautiful. I went down on my knees and elbows in the grass and said, out loud, that I was grateful for my life and for the world. I’ve only started doing this recently. I’m an atheist raised Catholic, I’d probably still call myself agnostic if pressed, but atheist is closer to true, including about Christianity specifically. And still I’ve picked up this habit of prayer and gratitude, and when I do it, I use Christ as the symbol I address it to. Make of that what you want. I haven’t fully sorted it out myself.
Shortly after, two young men started walking toward me from a distance. I clocked them as Latter-day Saints before they got close — they were both nineteen. Kind, earnest kids. I’ve decided to take that as a small sign from the universe that I need to stay more open to people regardless of what they believe. I add this story because again: The Denial of Death has started to change the way I see things. In addition to the Gospels of Christ and a few other important works.

The Hitler footnote

Late in the book there’s a footnote referencing a claim that Hitler’s mistresses used “be nice to him” as code for taking a shit on his head while he lay on the floor. Incredible and darkly funny if true. I did a lazy Google on it while reading and got the usual “just rumors, no evidence” response, so I went back and actually looked into where this comes from.
The claim traces almost entirely to one thread: Otto Strasser, a former Nazi Party insider turned Hitler opponent, told American intelligence officers in 1943 that he’d heard the story from Hitler’s niece, Geli Raubal, before her death in 1931. That interview fed into a 1943 OSS psychological profile of Hitler written by Harvard psychologist Walter C. Langer, which labeled Hitler an “impotent coprophile.” A separate OSS report that year, by psychologist Henry Murray, drew similar conclusions — though historians have since noted Langer’s report leaned heavily on Murray’s earlier work rather than standing as fully independent corroboration. There’s also a secondhand claim attributed to Ernst Röhm making a remark about Hitler’s tastes, but that’s fragmentary at best.
So it’s not really “multiple mistresses independently confirming it,” which is the version that would have made it convincing to me. It’s one secondhand account, filtered through a wartime propaganda-adjacent intelligence report, repeated by a couple of hostile witnesses whose motives historians treat with real skepticism. Historians like Bradley Smith, Hans Gatzke, and Martin Waugh have all gone on record calling the Langer report a “historical curiosity” at best — a wartime psychological-warfare product, not a documented fact. Mainstream Hitler biographers generally treat the whole episode as unproven.
I don’t need a photograph to believe something ugly about Hitler. But I was wrong to assume corroborating accounts existed. They mostly don’t — it’s one source, run through the rumor mill for eighty years. But do I believe it? Of course I do.

Why I’m doing this

I have a lot to learn here. If no one reads this, I’ll at least be spared the embarrassment of an audience watching me work through my own lack of formal education in public. But if you are reading — please comment. Tell me what I’m missing, what perspectives I should at least be aware of. I don’t think I’m the only person interested in this stuff in 2026. Read these books with me.
Next up is The Brothers Karamazov. I have my reasons for the books I picked and the order I’m reading them in — I’ll explain as I go. Thank you for reading.
